subject: Astronomy & Space
title: SETI: Listening for Signals
description: A micro-lesson that makes SETI: Listening for Signals usable.

hook.text: SETI—the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence—uses radio telescopes to listen for artificial signals from other stars.

buildup.text: The search began in 1960 when Frank Drake pointed a telescope at two nearby stars. He heard nothing—but the field was born.

discovery.text: In 1977, the 'Wow! signal' was detected—a strong, narrowband burst from space. It lasted 72 seconds and never repeated.

twist.text: Despite decades of listening, no confirmed alien signal has been found. But we've only searched a tiny fraction of the sky.

climax.text: Breakthrough Listen, funded with $100M in 2015, is the most comprehensive SETI program ever, scanning millions of stars.

punchline.text: Sixty years of listening. Nothing confirmed yet. But the search has barely begun.

quiz.question: What was the 'Wow! signal'?
options: A strong, unexplained radio burst detected in 1977 that lasted 72 seconds and never repeated
The first confirmed message from an alien civilization
A test signal sent by SETI to calibrate their radio telescopes

details.summary: The Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI) uses radio telescopes to scan the sky for artificial signals — narrow-band transmissions that natural sources cannot produce. Since Frank Drake's Project Ozma in 1960, SETI has listened to thousands of stars without confirmed detection.
details.whyItMatters: SETI represents humanity's most systematic effort to answer whether we're alone. Detecting even one artificial signal would be the most profound discovery in human history, confirming intelligence exists beyond Earth.
takeaways: SETI scans for artificial radio signals from other civilizations
Narrow-band signals would indicate technological origin
Thousands of stars have been searched without confirmed detection

faq.question: What was the Wow! Signal?
faq.answer: In 1977, astronomer Jerry Ehman detected a strong narrow-band radio signal lasting 72 seconds at the Big Ear telescope. He circled the printout and wrote 'Wow!' The signal matched expectations for an artificial extraterrestrial transmission but was never detected again despite repeated searches.

faq.question: How much of the sky has SETI searched?
faq.answer: Despite decades of searching, SETI has examined only a tiny fraction of the possible combinations of sky positions, frequencies, and signal types. It's been compared to searching a single glass of water for life in all Earth's oceans. The search has barely begun.
